```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  text <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  text <- gsub("//[^\n]*", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", text, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(text, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("ancient_iran_afghanistan_transcaucasia.json5")
sett_data <- fromJSON("ancient_iran_afghanistan_transcaucasia_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
ledger_data <- read_json5_clean("ancient_iran_afghanistan_transcaucasia_source_ledger.json5")
cache_data <- fromJSON("ancient_iran_afghanistan_transcaucasia_summary_cache.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)

fmt_eu_int <- function (x) {
  formatC(as.integer(round(as.numeric(x))), format = "d", big.mark = ".")
}

sett_countries <- vapply(sett_data, function (e) as.character(e[["country"]]), character(1))
cnt_tbl <- sort(table(sett_countries), decreasing = TRUE)
n_jur <- length(cnt_tbl)
tot_sites_n <- length(sett_data)

fmt_jur_shares <- function (tbl, total_n) {
  nms <- names(tbl)
  vals <- as.integer(tbl)
  sh <- vapply(vals, function (v) viscount_fmt_number(100 * v / total_n, 1L), character(1))
  parts <- paste0(nms, " (", vapply(vals, fmt_eu_int, character(1)), " sites, ", sh, "%)")
  if (length(parts) <= 1L) return(paste(parts, collapse = ""))
  paste0(paste(parts[-length(parts)], collapse = ", "), " and ", parts[length(parts)])
}

jur_share_str <- fmt_jur_shares(cnt_tbl, tot_sites_n)
```

# Abstract

This gazetteer documents 2.270 individually assessed ancient settlements, fortified tells, piedmont oasis towns and highland citadels active across Iran, Afghanistan, eastern Anatolia and Transcaucasia between 3200BC and 330BC, encompassing 37.831 five-arcminute cells across ten sub-regions. Compiled by reconciling published excavation monographs, regional surface surveys, the Near East Radiocarbon Database (NERD), the C-Turkey chronometric register, the Near East Holocene Urban Settlement Database (Palmisano et al. 2021), From Villages to Empires (Titolo and Palmisano 2025), the Stanford POLIS Greek *poleis* inventory and late-classical continuity anchors from the OXREP Roman Cities Database (Hanson 2016) [@Renette2023Historical; @Khorashadi2026Acropolis; @Dan2024Data; @Petrie2026Hills], the catalogue spans from lowland Proto-Elamite Susa and Chogha Mish to highland Anshan (Tall-e Malyan), Kerman craft centres at Konar Sandal, Shahdad and Tepe Yahya, Helmand delta hubs at Shahr-i Sokhta, Dahan-i Ghulaman and Mundigak, Urartian bastions at Tushpa, Ayanis, Korzut, Argishtikhinili and Erebuni, Pontic Trapezous, Median and Achaemenid capitals at Ecbatana, Rayy, Persepolis and Pasargadae, and eastern oasis metropolises at Balkh, Old Kandahar, Herat and Shortugai [@Wood2012After; @Munoz2013Problemas; @OZFIRAT2021Ernis]. Alongside the 2.270 individually assessed entries, the source ledger records 250 excluded subordinate suburbs and variant-spelling duplicates out of 2.520 evaluated candidates. Ranked by peak population, the 2.270 sites exhibit a steep polycentric Zipf hierarchy ($\alpha = 1,31$, $R^2 = 0,78$), reflecting the interplay of imperial capitals, satrapal centres, radiocarbon-dated tells and topographically bounded mountain valleys and desert-margin oases conditioned within geoBoundaries subadministrative frames [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries].

# Background

Settlement systems across ancient Iran, Afghanistan and Transcaucasia evolved around isolated water-bearing basins rather than a single continuous riverine corridor [@Petrie2026Hills; @Boucharlat2019Renewal]. In southwestern Khuzestan, the Karun and Dez alluvial fans hosted multi-tiered tells led by Susa and Chogha Mish from the fourth millennium BC onward, later joined by Middle Elamite monumental centres such as Chogha Zanbil and Haft Tappeh and highland Zagros nodes including Tall-e Malyan (Anshan), Tal-e Ghazir and Chogha Gavaneh [@Karaketir2023Elamtu; @Wicks2023Production; @Mohammadifar2025Redefining]. Across the arid interior of Kerman and Sistan, early urbanism concentrated along seasonal floodplains and piedmont springs at Konar Sandal, Tepe Yahya, Shahdad and Shahr-i Sokhta, before hydro-climatic shifts in the early second millennium BC prompted nucleation along more reliable river channels [@Petrie2026Hills; @Saatsaz2023Technology].

In the northern mountains, the Early Bronze Kura-Araxes horizon sustained agricultural tells such as Mokhrablur, Yanik Tepe and Ernis on Lake Van, evolving during the Late Bronze and Iron Ages into dense networks of cyclopean hillforts including Dmanisis Gora, Metsamor and Horom [@OZFIRAT2021Ernis; @Lindsay2026Towards; @Sevin2004Erken]. Under the Kingdom of Urartu (ninth to seventh centuries BC), state-built canals and fortified road stations linked Tushpa, Ayanis, Rusahinili, Korzut, Bastam, Argishtikhinili, Teishebaini and Erebuni across eastern Anatolia, the Aras valley and northwestern Iran, supplemented by upland bastions along the Hakkari frontier [@Cavusoglu2024Bianili; @Dan2024Data; @Gokce2021Lake; @COSKUN2026Hakkari]. Further south and east, the diffusion of gravity-fed qanats enabled Iron Age Median and Achaemenid towns—from Hasanlu, Godin Tepe, Ecbatana and Rayy to Persepolis, Pasargadae, Dahan-i Ghulaman, Old Kandahar, Herat and Balkh—to sustain dense populations along formerly arid gravel fans and Royal Road stages [@Saatsaz2021Water; @Mirghaderi2022Chronology; @Munoz2013Problemas; @Wood2012After].

# Methodology

## Compilation and Spatial Reconciliation

Each settlement entry in this gazetteer derives from a case-by-case archaeological and historical synthesis combining primary excavation monographs, regional surface surveys, the Near East Radiocarbon Database (NERD), the C-Turkey chronometric register, the Near East Holocene Urban Settlement Database (Palmisano et al. 2021), From Villages to Empires (Titolo and Palmisano 2025), Stanford POLIS and OXREP (Hanson 2016) continuity anchors, evaluated within the 2.520-entry chapter source ledger. Every retained site possesses verified WGS84 coordinates, an attributed modern jurisdiction, chronological occupation bounds spanning at least one benchmark between 3200BC and 330BC, and an evidence-assessed settlement-size trajectory derived from excavated mound area, intra-mural residential density and regional carrying-capacity ceilings [@Renette2023Historical; @Matthews2025Informatio].

To prevent multi-mound complexes and variant transliterations from distorting headcounts, the ledger enforces strict spatial deduplication: of 2.520 evaluated candidates, 250 were excluded as subordinate co-located localities within 3,2 km of a primary core or variant aliases within 25 km, retaining excluded records (such as Ayanis Kalesi, Baba Jan Tepe and Dinkha Tepe) in the ledger without double-counting urban totals.

## Subadministrative Alignment and Radial Weighting

Although ancient polities predated modern cadastral boundaries, every catalogued settlement is spatially indexed to geoBoundaries administrative polygons [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] across Iran, Afghanistan, Turkey, Armenia, Georgia and Azerbaijan. In HANDBOOK, point-level settlements act as spatial conditioning nodes for metric-isotropic radial distance fields and non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging, while strictly mass-conserving pycnophylactic scaling across 65.864 historical and modern subadministrative unit-year checks (maximum relative error $5,845 \times 10^{-8}$) bridges ancient catchment densities with Ottoman vilayet, Russian Imperial guberniya and modern ADM1/ADM2 census baselines [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries].

# Testing and Validation

Ledger reconciliation confirms exact accounting across all 2.520 evaluated candidates: 2.270 individually assessed primary settlements are included and 250 subordinate or duplicate records are excluded without discrepancy. Every catalogued settlement carries positive chronological estimates across the 3200BC to 330BC interval, with zero missing coordinates and zero unverified anachronisms. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} illustrates the domain rank-size distribution alongside the leading archaeological hubs.


# Results

## Leading Forty-Five Catalogued Settlements

Table \ref{tab:top45-iran} presents the top 45 individually assessed settlements ordered by peak population between 3200BC and 330BC. Rather than single-capital primacy, the macro-region exhibits a steep, multi-tiered polycentric Zipf hierarchy ($\alpha = 1,31$, $R^2 = 0,78$), anchored at the apex by six imperial and regional capitals exceeding 30k inhabitants: Ecbatana (62,4k in 400BC), Susa (61,2k in 400BC), Balkh (54,6k in 330BC), Persepolis (41,5k in 400BC), Anshan (36,5k in 2000BC) and Tushpa (33,8k in 680BC). Beneath this summit, twenty major satrapal capitals, Pontic foundations, Bronze Age desert-oasis metropolises and Urartian-Transcaucasian citadels—led by Old Kandahar (26,2k), Shahr-i Sokhta (24,8k), Rayy (23,6k), Herat (23,4k), Konar Sandal (20,4k), Dahan-i Ghulaman (17,2k), Argishtikhinili (15,4k), Mtskheta (15,4k) and Trapezous (11,8k)—surpass 10k inhabitants at their respective chronological peaks [@Petrie2026Hills; @Khorashadi2026Acropolis; @Bartelmus2025Chapter].

```{r tab-top45, results='asis'}
fmt_coord <- function(x) gsub("[.]", ",", format(round(as.numeric(x), 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE))
fmt_bc_year <- function(y) paste0(abs(as.integer(y)), "BC")

peaks <- vapply(sett_data, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
ord <- order(peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_n <- min(45L, length(ord))

rows <- lapply(sett_data[ord[seq_len(top_n)]], function(e) {
  yrs <- as.integer(names(e[["population"]]))
  pks <- as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))
  pk_y <- names(e[["population"]])[which.max(pks)]
  pk_v <- max(pks)
  span_str <- if (length(yrs) == 1L) {
    fmt_bc_year(yrs[1])
  } else {
    paste0(fmt_bc_year(min(yrs)), " to ", fmt_bc_year(max(yrs)))
  }
  data.frame(
    Settlement = e[["name"]],
    Country = e[["country"]],
    Coords = paste0(fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[1]]), ", ", fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[2]])),
    Span = span_str,
    Peak = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pk_v), " (", fmt_bc_year(pk_y), ")"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
top_df <- do.call(rbind, rows)
rownames(top_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  top_df,
  "Top 45 individually assessed ancient settlements across Iran, Afghanistan and Transcaucasia ordered by peak population (2.270 total sites).",
  c("Settlement", "Jurisdiction", "Lat, Lon", "Occupation Span", "Peak (Year)"),
  list(label = "tab:top45-iran", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 30L)
)
```

## Distribution by Modern Jurisdiction

Table \ref{tab:country-sum-iran} aggregates the 2.270 individually assessed settlements across the `r n_jur` modern jurisdictions intersecting the chapter domain: `r jur_share_str`. Leading regional centres span from 8,8k at Qabala in Azerbaijan and 15,4k at both Argishtikhinili in Armenia and Mtskheta in Georgia to 33,8k at Tushpa in eastern Turkey, 54,6k at Balkh in Afghanistan and 62,4k at Ecbatana in Iran, confirming that substantial urban and fortress hierarchies developed across the macro-region prior to 330BC [@Dan2024Data; @Lindsay2026Towards; @Wood2012After].

```{r tab-country-sum, results='asis'}
countries <- sort(unique(vapply(sett_data, function(e) e[["country"]], character(1))))
tot_sites <- length(sett_data)

sum_rows <- lapply(countries, function(cn) {
  sub_e <- Filter(function(e) identical(e[["country"]], cn), sett_data)
  pks <- vapply(sub_e, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
  idx_m <- which.max(pks)
  lead <- sub_e[[idx_m]]
  yrs <- names(lead[["population"]])
  pk_y <- yrs[which.max(as.numeric(unlist(lead[["population"]])))]
  data.frame(
    Country = cn,
    Sites = viscount_fmt_number(length(sub_e), 0L),
    Share = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(100 * length(sub_e) / tot_sites, 1L), "%"),
    Lead = lead[["name"]],
    Peak = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pks[idx_m]), " (", abs(as.integer(pk_y)), "BC)"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sum_df <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)
sum_df <- sum_df[order(-as.numeric(gsub("[.]", "", sum_df$Sites))), ]
rownames(sum_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sum_df,
  paste0("Individually assessed settlement counts, territorial share and leading centres across ", n_jur, " modern jurisdictions (2.270 total sites)."),
  c("Jurisdiction", "Assessed Sites", "Share", "Leading Centre", "Peak (Year)"),
  list(label = "tab:country-sum-iran", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Limitations

Two spatial and archaeological caveats affect the settlement register. First, modern national borders bisect several integrated ancient settlement networks—notably dividing Urartian fortresses across eastern Turkey, Armenia and northwestern Iran, and splitting the Helmand and Drangiana oases between Iranian Sistan and southern Afghanistan—so jurisdiction totals in Table \ref{tab:country-sum-iran} reflect modern geoBoundaries polygons rather than ancient polity frontiers [@OZFIRAT2021Ernis; @Dan2024Data; @Runfola2020GeoBoundaries]. Because kriging catchments and sub-regional population masks integrate across biophysical basins rather than modern borders, regional demographic totals remain unaffected.

Second, site recovery reflects uneven historical excavation intensity [@Boucharlat2019Renewal; @Gokce2021Lake]. Western Iran, Susiana, Fars and the Lake Van littoral benefit from dense pedestrian survey coverage, whereas rugged upland valleys in Afghanistan and the Greater Caucasus remain under-sampled, particularly for small rural hamlets beneath deep colluvial or alluvial fans [@Petrie2026Hills].

# Conclusion

The 2.270 individually assessed settlements catalogued here trace the shift from fourth-millennium Proto-Elamite riverine towns and Bronze Age desert-delta hubs to Iron Age mountain fortresses and Achaemenid royal-road capitals. By documenting both retained primary centres and 250 consolidated subordinate suburbs and variant aliases within a single audited source ledger, the gazetteer supplies a clean, non-redundant documentary anchor for demographic mapping across ancient Iran, Afghanistan and Transcaucasia to 330BC [@Renette2023Historical; @Saatsaz2023Technology; @Munoz2013Problemas].

# Appendix

## Source Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:excluded-iran} lists the leading 30 of 250 excluded candidate records in the regional source ledger, consolidated into primary urban cores during proximity filtering within 3,2 km or alias deduplication within 25 km.

```{r tab-excluded, results='asis'}
exc_list <- Filter(function(c) identical(c[["status"]], "excluded"), ledger_data[["candidates"]])
exc_n <- min(30L, length(exc_list))

map_reason <- function(r) {
  if (is.null(r) || !nzchar(r)) return("Duplicate alias")
  if (identical(r, "subordinate_suburb_merged")) return("Subordinate suburb")
  if (identical(r, "duplicate_alias")) return("Duplicate alias")
  gsub("_", " ", r)
}

map_action <- function(r) {
  if (identical(r, "duplicate_alias")) return("Deduplicated variant alias within 25 km")
  "Merged within 3,2 km buffer of primary core"
}

exc_rows <- lapply(exc_list[seq_len(exc_n)], function(c) {
  data.frame(
    Candidate = c[["name"]],
    Country = c[["country"]],
    Classification = map_reason(c[["reason"]]),
    Consolidation = map_action(c[["reason"]]),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
exc_df <- do.call(rbind, exc_rows)
rownames(exc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  exc_df,
  "Leading 30 of 250 excluded candidate entries in the chapter source ledger consolidated into primary urban cores.",
  c("Candidate Site", "Jurisdiction", "Classification", "Consolidation Action"),
  list(label = "tab:excluded-iran", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```
